title: The Ring in the Drawer
text:
My grandmother kept a small wooden box in the bottom drawer of her desk. Inside it was a ring so [[ancient]] that nobody in our family knew who had made it.

She wore it only twice a year. The rest of the time the box stayed shut, and the ring sat in the dark like an [[ordinary]] piece of metal. But to her it was the most [[precious]] thing she owned.

"Is it [[valuable]]?" I asked her once. She laughed and said a shop would give her very little for it. Then she went [[silent]] for a moment.

The ring had belonged to her mother, who stayed [[single]] until she was thirty — [[rare]] in those days. In her [[youth]] that woman had worked in a tea factory, and she saved for eleven years to buy it.

"When I hold it," my grandmother said, "she is still [[alive]] to me."

Every Lunar New Year my grandmother put on her [[traditional]] blue dress and wore the ring for the [[whole]] day. Aunts and cousins filled the house; she stood at the door as the [[host]] and welcomed every [[guest]] with both hands.

Last winter she gave the box to me. I am not a careful girl, and I was afraid of losing something so [[personal]] to her.

"Wear it," she said. "A ring in a drawer helps nobody."

Now it sits on my finger, a little loose, and I catch myself touching it on the bus. It is not a [[perfect]] ring; part of the silver has worn thin. But when I look down at it, two women I never met are standing beside me.

title: The Busiest Shop on the Street
topic: 人物・形容詞・小吃店
text:
The noodle shop at the corner opens at six in the morning. By seven it is already [[crowded]], and by noon the line reaches the bus stop.

Mr. Kao has run it for thirty years with his wife, who is also his business [[partner]]. He cooks; she takes the money and remembers every [[customer]] by name.

The kitchen is small and terribly [[noisy]] — pots, steam, the radio, and Mr. Kao shouting orders at nobody in particular. Watching him work is like watching a [[skillful]] driver in heavy traffic. Nothing is wasted. His father taught him, and people in the market still call the old man a [[master]].

Their beef noodles are [[fantastic]], but that is not the [[main]] reason people come. It is the [[pleasant]] feeling of being known. Mrs. Kao will ask about your mother's knee, your examination, your new job.

Only two tables are [[available]] before eight, so most people eat standing up. Nobody complains. The service is nearly [[instant]]: you sit down, and the bowl arrives.

My father has been a [[regular]] there since he was in high school. He says the taste has not changed in forty years, which is [[impossible]], but I have never argued with him about it.

Last year Mr. Kao was sick for a month and the shop stayed shut. The street felt wrong without the steam and the shouting. When he came back, a [[lady]] from the flower stall put a small plant on the counter. She did not say a word. She did not need to.

title: The Boy Who Came Back
text:
A new student joined our class in October. His family had lived [[overseas]] for six years, and for the first week he sat [[alone]] at the back of the room, saying almost nothing.

Our teacher told us he was [[homesick]], which sounded strange to me. He had come home, had he not? But home for him was a cold northern city where the buses ran on time and nobody asked where he was from.

His Chinese was correct but oddly [[formal]], like a news reader on the radio. Whenever he answered a question, the whole class went quiet and his face turned red.

Then one Friday our science teacher wrote a hard problem on the board. Nobody moved. The new boy walked up and solved it in four lines. Somebody at the front whispered that he was a [[genius]]. He sat down quickly, as if he had done something wrong.

After that, things changed in a [[sudden]] way. Two boys from the basketball team asked him to play. He was slow and he missed a lot, but by December he had become a [[responsible]] player who never skipped practice.

I asked him once whether he wanted to go back. He thought for a long time and then gave a [[negative]] answer.

"It was a [[peaceful]] place," he said, "but for six years I was a [[visitor]] there. Here people argue with me."

His mother says he is more [[independent]] now. He is also the most [[likely]] person in our class to become a scientist, and he holds the door for the [[adult]] teachers until every one of them has passed. My mother met him once and called him a little [[gentleman]].

Our lives are more [[similar]] than I ever thought.
